event: VXE-641 rolled left, departed controlled flight and spiraled into the ground from an 800 ft AGL fixed-wing orbit 1 hour 7 minutes into a mission; aircraft lost (CAT 5).
failure_mode: sudden step roll rate bias of about 20 deg/s on the FWAP gyro, beyond what the AHRS can converge out (about 5 deg/s), so FWAP estimated roll right while the aircraft rolled left
contributing: FWAP gyro is a single point of failure; FW and VTOL attitude solutions are only cross-checked during preflight and climb-out
gyro tested normal in the lab afterwards, so the fault was transient

evidence.quote: VTOL attitude estimate shows roll left matching reports, while fixed-wing ap shows roll going to the right.
Gyro measurements from FWAP show a roll rate bias of about 20 deg/s around the time of the event.
Whatever happened to the gyro looks like something transient during the flight.
Fixed-wing autopilot roll gyro suddenly developed a bias of approximately 20 deg/s.
FWAP and VTOL gyros are synced during takeoff, indicating issue was not present when preflight and takeoff checks were performed.

team_root_cause: FWAP Gyro Bias caused AHRS to report an inaccurate roll.  That in turn caused the vehicle to depart controlled flight and crash.

would_settle_it.what: FWAP versus VTOL roll and roll rate plot showing the step bias at the event
component level failure analysis of the gyro to find why it read a transient bias

reasoning: The FWAP and VTOL autopilots disagreed on roll direction at the event, and the FWAP gyro shows a roll rate bias of about 20 deg/s against the VTOL gyro. A simulation showed a bias that size drives the AHRS unstable, matching the flight. Both gyros agreed at takeoff, and the unit read normal in the lab later, so this was a transient in-flight gyro fault whose physical cause is not known.
notes: RMA-946 is linked but not in the export; it would only add intake and repair status. Lab test found yaw drift without magnetometer, which engineers explained as normal.

event: VXE-920 (Adv Nav, battery) had a 35 second downlink loss in fixed-wing flight over the ocean; the GCS automatically commanded Land Immediately, the aircraft hovered with lift power faults until the HLB ran out and it glided into the ocean; aircraft lost.
failure_mode: LandOnError=1 in gcs.ini made the GCS issue an automatic Land Immediately when downlink was lost, with no confirmation and no altitude or energy check, over water far from a landing site
contributing: GCS internal default for LandOnError was enabled (unsafe default, fixed in GCS 6.7.0)
automatic Land Immediately bypasses the too-high altitude warning used for operator commanded Land Immediately
intermittent downlink in a jamming area
during the long hover the VTOL logged repeated lift system min power faults (climb abort) until battery depletion

evidence.quote: [19:10:24.485 7500.485] ap link fault: local rx okay ap rx bad
[19:11:00.564 7536.564] ap dbg: vt lnd now request
from GCS debug logs it appears that the GCS issued 3 land immediately commands due to loss of downlink.
I’ve tested the theory that gcs.ini was deleted and restored and this does not appear to be a plausible explanation.
Further code inspection has revealed it is nearly impossible for the GCS to overwrite LandOnError=0 with LandOnError=1 so it seems like the file must have been changed by someone
[19:14:26.270 7742.270] DebugMsg Climb abort, lift system fault

team_root_cause: Mismatch of behavior between gcs.ini settings and default hardcoded into GCS.  Deleting gcs.ini or removing LandOnError from the INI caused the system to revert to an unsafe LandOnError=1 state.
disagreement: The GCS auto Land Immediately from LandOnError=1 is agreed, but the Root Cause field blames ini deletion reverting to the hardcoded default. The engineer's own later test says "this does not appear to be a plausible explanation" and that "the file must have been changed by someone", so how LandOnError=1 got into gcs.ini is not established.

would_settle_it.what: file timestamps and install history showing when and how LandOnError=1 was written
vtFaults, vtThr1 to vtThr4 and HLB voltage during the 30 minute hover to show why the aircraft did not complete the descent

reasoning: The XCOMM event log shows a downlink fault at 7500 s, link restored at 7535 s and a land-now request one second later, and the GCS debug log shows the GCS issued Land Immediately commands because of the downlink loss. The GCS does this only when LandOnError is enabled, which it was in the incident gcs.ini. The aircraft then hovered with repeated lift power faults until the battery was exhausted and it went into the ocean. Who or what set LandOnError=1 is not settled.
